scope_note: Daily edition from matching Tuesday /new listings: 269 non-replacement cs.CV rows, 104 cs.RO rows, 355 deduplicated papers, and 291 ROI papers. Tier A cards are conservative abstract-only autopsies from the repository parser output; no figure, table, or full-text claims are asserted.
executive_thesis: The August 18 batch pushes robot intelligence toward runtime evidence control. VLAs add process rewards, tactile residuals, counterfactual recovery, stop-aware chunking, and test-time computation; maps become task-conditioned Gaussian or LiDAR memories that decide what to update, ignore, or relight; and deployment benchmarks move toward multi-view, flood, driving, and embodied safety harnesses that preserve the physical condition behind each claim.

decision_cards.label: Decision
decision_cards.title: VLA authority moves to runtime interfaces
decision_cards.body: CoRe, ViTaR, Robo-Dopamine 2.0, SparkVLA, and tau0-VLA all expose an intermediate recovery, contact, reward, stop, or search interface that can change the next robot action.

decision_cards.label: Decision
decision_cards.title: Maps are becoming selective control memories
decision_cards.body: SpotlessGS, MotionGS-SLAM, geometry-aware 3DGS mapping, GaussMemory, and HP2-SLAM ask when a map should relight, blur-model, allocate density, remember task objects, or rely on ICP.

decision_cards.label: Decision
decision_cards.title: Benchmarks preserve physical evidence
decision_cards.body: FloodReasonBench, CrossView, ScenarioCharacterization, MM-BEV, HarnessEval-W, and embodied-agent security work make the evaluated evidence path part of the deployment claim.

papers.title: Imagining Recovery: Inference-Time Counterfactual Realignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.fit: VLA recovery - counterfactual rollout - training-free realignment
papers.status_quo: A deployed VLA is usually expected to continue from the current observation or require failure data, retraining, or an external recovery agent.
papers.friction: Mid-episode goal changes, scene perturbations, and robot-state deviations can break a frozen policy even when a recent viable state still exists.
papers.hidden_premise: A synthetic continuation from a viable state can supply enough evidence to realign the physical robot without unsafe trial-and-error.
papers.conceptual_move: Treat recovery as counterfactual realignment: imagine the nominal continuation, minimally move robot and scene back onto it, then return control to the frozen policy.
papers.mechanism: The abstract describes detecting deviation, synthesizing observations from a recent viable state, and realigning the robot and scene before policy handoff.

evidence.claim: CoRe is a training-free framework that recovers a frozen VLA at inference time without failure data.
The authors report improved success and reduced physical restorations across simulators, VLA backbones, and real-world settings.
APRL should measure whether imagined recovery changes the next action before more physical correction is attempted.

papers.falsification: If counterfactual continuations only help small geometric perturbations but fail under contact-rich state uncertainty, the recovery authority is narrower than the headline suggests.
papers.adversarial: Stress false deviation detection, ambiguous viable states, and cases where the imagined observation is plausible but contact state is wrong.
papers.thinking_tool: Recover by testing the action path that should have happened, not by immediately retraining or handing control away.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for frozen VLA deployment with recoverable state deviations; weaker where the viable state is not observable or safe to reconstruct.

papers.title: ViTaR: Visuo-Tactile Residual Adaptation for Foundation VLA Manipulation
papers.fit: contact-rich manipulation - tactile residuals - bounded adaptation
papers.status_quo: Foundation VLAs encode broad visual-semantic priors but often treat contact as hidden state or let tactile feedback directly rewrite action generation.
papers.friction: The same visual state can require different actions when contact is established, lost, or destabilized.
papers.hidden_premise: Tactile feedback should have bounded residual authority rather than unbounded control over the policy.
papers.conceptual_move: Reframe tactile sensing from a primary action-generating input into an execution-layer residual that corrects a VLA when contact evidence demands it.
papers.mechanism: The abstract positions tactile residual adaptation as a way to keep VLA priors while adding local contact sensitivity.

evidence.claim: The paper names contact-rich deployment as a blind spot for foundation VLA manipulation.
It argues against both internal VLA modification and unbounded tactile influence over actions.
APRL should separate visual-semantic intent from contact residual authority in manipulation evaluation.

papers.falsification: If tactile residuals improve success only by overriding the VLA on most steps, the method is not a bounded adaptation layer.
papers.adversarial: Use contact loss, false tactile events, slippery objects, and visually identical contact states to test whether residual authority is calibrated.
papers.thinking_tool: Give contact a veto or correction channel, not a blank check to replace the policy.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for tactile manipulation; less direct for tasks where critical state is visual or proprioceptive rather than contact-based.

papers.title: Robo-Dopamine 2.0: History-Conditioned and OOD-Aware Process Reward Modeling for Robotic Manipulation
papers.fit: process reward - history conditioning - OOD manipulation failure
papers.status_quo: Robot RL refinement often relies on sparse terminal success or static before-after visual rewards.
papers.friction: Static rewards cannot distinguish robust variations from task-invalid off-trajectory behavior under scene changes and compounding errors.
papers.hidden_premise: A reward model needs execution history and an OOD-sensitive comparison interface to score progress rather than appearance.
papers.conceptual_move: Turn visual reward modeling into a process assessment problem conditioned on trajectory history and distribution shift.
papers.mechanism: The abstract introduces a history- and OOD-aware process reward model with a pairwise prediction interface.

evidence.claim: The paper states that learned visual reward models relying on static before-after observations suffer temporal ambiguity.
It proposes history-conditioned and OOD-aware process reward modeling for robotic manipulation.
APRL should evaluate whether a reward curve predicts recoverable deviation before terminal failure.

papers.falsification: If history conditioning correlates mainly with video length or scene identity, it may reward dataset artifacts instead of progress.
papers.adversarial: Compare trajectories with the same start and end frames but different contact mistakes, recovery paths, and object-state histories.
papers.thinking_tool: Use the shape of a trajectory as reward evidence, not just its first and last frames.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for long-horizon manipulation refinement; weaker for simple tasks with unambiguous terminal labels.

papers.title: GaussMemory: Task-Driven 3D Gaussian Scene Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.fit: 3D Gaussian memory - task-driven update - long-horizon manipulation
papers.status_quo: 3D robot memories are often passive recorders that update visible elements through fixed rules.
papers.friction: A background wall and a grasp target should not receive the same update budget during long-horizon manipulation.
papers.hidden_premise: A robot can learn what to remember, update, or discard from task success rather than from hand-designed map heuristics.
papers.conceptual_move: Make 3D Gaussian scene memory task-driven: memory management becomes part of the manipulation policy's evidence contract.
papers.mechanism: The abstract argues for end-to-end learning of object precision, update aggressiveness, and discard behavior.

evidence.claim: The paper says existing 3D memory systems treat critical objects and irrelevant background with equal importance.
It proposes active, task-driven spatial memory for long-horizon robotic manipulation.
APRL should score map memory by whether it preserves the object state that changes the next manipulation step.

papers.falsification: If learned memory improves rendering but not action recovery after occlusion or rearrangement, it is not task-driven enough.
papers.adversarial: Use distractor objects, occluded targets, and task switches where remembering the wrong object actively hurts the policy.
papers.thinking_tool: Treat memory update as a control decision with a downstream task metric.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for object-centric manipulation; weaker for pure localization where every geometric feature may carry tracking value.

papers.title: MotionGS-SLAM: Event-Modulated Gaussian Splatting for Motion-Blur Robust SLAM
papers.fit: 3DGS SLAM - event camera - motion blur robustness
papers.status_quo: Vision SLAM often treats motion blur as degraded input that should be restored before mapping.
papers.friction: Deblurring is ill-posed, and catastrophic tracking failure can occur when fast motion destroys frame-based evidence.
papers.hidden_premise: Event timing can constrain blur formation directly inside the Gaussian rendering and mapping model.
papers.conceptual_move: Move from removing blur artifacts to forward-modeling blur with event-modulated Gaussian rasterization.
papers.mechanism: The abstract describes an event-modulated Gaussian kernel that adapts rasterization using microsecond event evidence.

evidence.claim: The paper says current vision SLAM can fail catastrophically under motion blur.
It reformulates blur handling as a constrained forward problem inside the rendering pipeline.
APRL should compare event-constrained maps against frame-only maps under controlled angular velocity and lighting.

papers.falsification: If gains vanish when blur is paired with low texture or dynamic objects, event modulation may only solve one degradation channel.
papers.adversarial: Stress fast camera rotation, low light, sparse event rates, and moving objects separately.
papers.thinking_tool: When perception is degraded, model the sensor failure mode rather than pretending the clean observation exists.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for event-camera SLAM; weaker for robots without asynchronous sensing.

papers.title: FloodReasonBench: Benchmarking VLM Reasoning Segmentation for Embodied Flood Response at the Edge
papers.fit: flood response - reasoning segmentation - edge embodied benchmark
papers.status_quo: Reasoning segmentation benchmarks usually use generic visual scenes and ignore resource-constrained disaster response.
papers.friction: An embodied flood-response agent must ground mission language in water, roads, people, and hazards under edge compute limits.
papers.hidden_premise: A benchmark is useful for embodied response only if task accuracy and resource constraints are measured together.
papers.conceptual_move: Specialize reasoning segmentation into a flood-response benchmark with response-relevant targets and edge deployment constraints.
papers.mechanism: The abstract introduces FloodResponseSeg and evaluates VLM reasoning segmentation beyond generic scenes.

evidence.claim: The paper states that existing benchmarks overlook flood-response domain and resource constraints.
It builds a flood-specific reasoning-segmentation dataset from real-world scenes and response-relevant targets.
APRL should pair grounding accuracy with latency and action-critical hazard misses.

papers.falsification: If flood-specific labels do not change route, rescue, or inspection decisions, the benchmark may remain perception-only.
papers.adversarial: Evaluate small hazards, reflective water, occluded roads, and cases where the most salient object is not the action-critical one.
papers.thinking_tool: A disaster benchmark should say which grounded pixel changes a physical response.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for edge embodied perception and field robotics; less direct for indoor manipulation.

papers.title: CrossView: Can Vision-Language Models Reason Across Cameras?
papers.status_quo: Video VLM benchmarks often assume one camera stream and treat more frames as the main scaling variable.
papers.friction: Real robots, vehicles, and security systems observe with simultaneous views where the needed evidence may exist only in a subset of cameras.
papers.hidden_premise: A VLM must choose and fuse camera evidence, not merely process a longer visual context.
papers.conceptual_move: Reframe video understanding as cross-camera evidence selection under overlap, occlusion, and divergent perspectives.
papers.mechanism: The abstract argues that multi-camera reasoning is fundamentally different from single-camera video understanding and that current models struggle.

evidence.claim: The paper says multi-camera reasoning must resolve occlusions, decide which views matter, and integrate overlapping or diverging evidence.
It reports that current models struggle with this setting.
APRL should report which camera changed the decision in a multi-view robot or driving task.

papers.falsification: If failures are caused mostly by token length rather than view selection, the benchmark is a context-compression test rather than cross-view reasoning.
papers.adversarial: Use scenes where one camera is misleading, delayed, or occluded while another contains the decisive safety evidence.
papers.thinking_tool: Ask which viewpoint earns decision authority before fusing all views.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for multi-camera robots and driving; less direct for single-camera policies.

papers.title: Evidence of Absence: Cross-Modal Abductive Risk Perception to Sustain World Models When Vision Fails
papers.fit: world model risk - missing visual evidence - cross-modal abduction
papers.status_quo: World-state models assume visual observations populate entities, relations, context, and predictive cues.
papers.friction: Occlusion or visual degradation can remove exactly the evidence a robot needs to preserve risk predictions.
papers.hidden_premise: The absence of expected co-evidence from one modality can itself indicate a hidden cause when a complementary modality remains informative.
papers.conceptual_move: Sustain the world model through abductive cross-modal risk perception, instantiated with acoustic cues when vision fails.
papers.mechanism: The abstract describes microphone-array bearing and approach-rate evidence used when the primary visual modality is occluded or degraded.

evidence.claim: The paper asks how to sustain a structured world-state model when visual observations are missing.
It treats absence of expected co-evidence as evidence of a hidden cause and instantiates the idea acoustically.
APRL should evaluate whether missing visual evidence changes the stop, search, or avoidance action.

papers.falsification: If acoustic evidence only recovers already obvious risks, abduction does not add control value.
papers.adversarial: Stress silent hazards, reflective visual clutter, delayed audio, and cases where absence indicates sensor failure rather than hidden object risk.
papers.thinking_tool: Missing evidence can be an action-relevant observation when the expected co-evidence should have appeared.
papers.transfer_boundary: Strong for degraded perception and mobile robots; weaker for tasks where complementary modalities are unavailable.

synthesis.title: VLA adaptation is becoming authority allocation
synthesis.facts: The selected papers expose recovery imagination, tactile residuals, process rewards, stop-prefix ranking, and world-model-guided search as separate authority channels.
synthesis.inference: APRL should compare which channel changes a next action under the same perturbation before trusting terminal success gains.

synthesis.title: Robot maps now need update stop conditions
synthesis.facts: The batch asks maps to handle task relevance, motion blur, illumination, LiDAR degeneracy, and sensor changes rather than only maximize reconstruction quality.
synthesis.inference: A map representation should be judged by when it updates, refuses evidence, or changes a downstream action.

synthesis.title: Evaluation is moving toward evidence provenance
synthesis.links: FloodReasonBench - CrossView - ScenarioCharacterization - HarnessEval-W - embodied security
synthesis.facts: The benchmark papers preserve domain, camera, scenario, resource, or trust-boundary evidence as part of the claimed result.
synthesis.inference: Deployment evaluation should explain which physical evidence path supports the score and which missing path would falsify it.

frontier_memory.label: Strengthening
frontier_memory.history: August 17 emphasized commitment interfaces for tool use, process judging, world-model predicates, and matched safety events.
frontier_memory.body: August 18 strengthens the same commitment-before-action axis with tactile residual authority, counterfactual recovery, stop-aware action chunks, task-driven Gaussian memory, and multi-camera evidence selection.

frontier_memory.label: New signal
frontier_memory.history: Recent geometry notes focused on map quality, localization, and event or LiDAR efficiency.
frontier_memory.body: Today adds a sharper map-governance question: when should a Gaussian or LiDAR map allocate density, relight, reject blur, remember task objects, or stop updating?

frontier_memory.label: Missing axis
frontier_memory.history: Prior RI editions repeatedly called for robot-usable geometry and safety diagnostics.
frontier_memory.body: The current batch still lacks one shared benchmark that joins contact residuals, map update choices, multi-view evidence, and recovery authority inside the same closed-loop robot task.

strategy.title: Runtime-authority VLA benchmark
strategy.thesis: Measure which runtime interface is allowed to alter, delay, or veto a VLA action under the same perturbation.
strategy.one_week: Run two manipulation tasks with object displacement, contact loss, and mid-episode instruction change; compare counterfactual recovery, tactile residuals, process rewards, and stop-aware chunking.
strategy.four_week: Build a reusable harness that swaps recovery, residual, reward, stop, and test-time search modules around the same frozen VLA backbone.
strategy.success: At least one interface predicts or prevents a failure earlier than terminal success while preserving non-perturbed success.
strategy.stop: All interfaces rank episodes the same way as final success and cannot identify which next action should change.
strategy.asset: Perturbation suite, action deltas, contact states, recovery proposals, reward curves, stop-prefix choices, and veto outcomes.

strategy.title: Task-driven Gaussian map governance
strategy.thesis: Turn Gaussian and LiDAR mapping from passive reconstruction into a policy for update, relight, reject, remember, and discard decisions.
strategy.one_week: Create a small scene set with dynamic lighting, camera motion blur, distractor objects, LiDAR degeneracy, and task-relevant occlusions.
strategy.four_week: Compare SpotlessGS-style relighting, event-modulated blur modeling, geometry-aware density control, task-driven memory, and hybrid ICP under identical robot tasks.
strategy.success: A map-update policy improves localization or manipulation recovery under at least two degradation families without increasing false stable memories.
strategy.stop: Map governance only improves visual metrics and does not change downstream robot decisions.
strategy.asset: Degraded multi-view scenes, event/LiDAR streams, Gaussian update traces, task object masks, and downstream action outcomes.

strategy.title: Physical-evidence benchmark provenance
strategy.thesis: Make every score identify the camera, modality, scenario field, resource budget, or trust boundary that supports the deployment claim.
strategy.one_week: Choose one flood-response, driving, or indoor navigation task and mark which view, modality, scenario variable, and edge budget is decisive for action.
strategy.four_week: Evaluate VLM segmentation, cross-view reasoning, scenario characterization, timely BEV perception, and embodied-agent attacks using the same provenance schema.
strategy.success: The provenance schema exposes a model ranking reversal or a safety failure hidden by the aggregate score.
strategy.stop: The provenance fields do not predict action errors beyond ordinary held-out accuracy.
strategy.asset: Scenario cards, view-authority labels, modality-degradation cases, edge-budget traces, trust-boundary attacks, and action-impact annotations.
